newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Metals - Japan market quiet, LME seen firm.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Japan market quiet, LME seen firm.

text.p: Japanese base metal premiums held mostly steady in the past week and the physical market was quiet, while traders eyed the latest moves on the London Metal Exchange amid growing expectations that prices may firm.

LME three-month copper prices rallied overnight to the top of their recent range, settling $43 higher at $1,948 per tonne. Japanese traders now expect a challenge of resistance at $1,970, a level breached only once in the past month.
With the renewed strength in copper, there were also cautious expectations that aluminium prices may finally begin forming a base after the steady slide of the past month.

"(Copper) inventories are still continuing to fall," said one source at a large trade house, noting that LME warehouse stocks have fallen steadily in recent weeks after building up in August. "I'm hearing that Europe is extremely tight."
He added, however, that resistance at $1,970 to $1,980 would be difficult to overcome.
Another trader said the rally appeared largely technical in nature, although he also expected a near-term test of $1,970.
The firmness in copper prompted a few traders to suggest, cautiously, that aluminium prices may also be ready to start forming a base after recent tumbles.
The LME aluminium price has been on a steady slide since January 1995, when a year-long rally peaked just short of $2,200 a tonne.
The market has shifted into a particularly steep downtrend in the past month, tumbling from a high of $1,520 a tonne on September 2 to Monday's two-and-a-half-year low of $1,332.

Traders cited signs of a pick-up in physical business in the United States and Europe as possible sources of support for aluminium prices, although one warned: "The inertia of this bearish market is still taking its toll."
Another added that the market may now try to establish a base at the $1,330 level.

Japanese traders saw few signs of activity in the physical market, noting that a Japanese holiday on Thursday and the absence of some participants who were attending the annual LME dinner in London this week contributed to the markets' quiet tone.

One copper trader said the supply tightness of the past few months appeared to have eased, with premiums edging lower. He doubted Japanese users would be willing to pay premiums of more than $70.
Another trader added, however, that scrap availability was still limited and some tightness might continue through next month.

In the aluminium market, users were said to be mostly sidelined as they waited for LME prices to bottom out, although Tuesday's brief strengthening of the yen encouraged some buying for fourth-quarter delivery, traders said.
